definition: A separate line of work inside a repository. You make your changes on a branch so the main code stays safe until your work is reviewed.
Download a copy of a repository from GitHub to your own computer so you can work on it.
A saved snapshot of your changes, with a short message that explains what you changed.
Anyone who improves a project: by writing code, fixing docs, reporting bugs, designing, or reviewing.
Your own copy of someone else's repository, stored under your GitHub account. You push your changes to your fork, then ask the original project to accept them.
A tool that tracks every change made to a set of files, so you can see the history, undo mistakes, and work with others.
A website where people store Git repositories online and work on them together through issues and pull requests.
A post on a repository that describes a bug, a task, or an idea. Contributors usually pick an issue before starting work.
A tag on an issue or pull request that tells you what kind of work it is, like good first issue or documentation.
A person who looks after a project: they review pull requests, answer questions, and decide what gets merged.
Combine the changes from one branch into another. When a maintainer merges your pull request, your work becomes part of the project.
Software whose code is public, so anyone can read it, use it, and suggest improvements.
Download the latest changes from a remote repository into your local copy.
A request asking the maintainers to review your changes and merge them into the project. Often shortened to PR.
Upload your local commits to a repository on GitHub, usually your fork.
The first file people read in a repository. It explains what the project is and how to get started.
A project folder tracked by Git, including all its files and their full history. Often shortened to repo.
When someone reads your pull request and leaves comments, suggestions, or an approval before it is merged.
